prompt: Some countries are considering reducing the standard working week from five days to four, with no reduction in pay. Do the advantages of this change outweigh the disadvantages?
essay:
Reducing the standard week to four days without cutting pay is no longer a fringe proposal, and a number of employers have now tried it. In my view the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, but the case rests on an empirical claim that does not hold everywhere.

The argument in favour is not really about happiness. It is that a substantial part of a five-day week is not productive: hours spent in meetings that exist because there is time for them, and attention that has degraded by the fourth consecutive day. Trials in office-based organisations have generally reported that output held steady, which suggests the fifth day was buying less than the payroll implied. The benefits to employees are then genuine additions rather than a transfer — more recovery time, fewer commuting days, and a workforce that is measurably less exhausted.

The difficulty is that this reasoning is specific to a kind of work. Where output is a direct function of hours present — a ward, a production line, a delivery round — removing a day removes the corresponding output, and the only way to maintain the service is to hire more people at the same wage. For those employers the change is simply a large increase in labour costs. There is a further complication: compressing five days of work into four is not the same policy at all, and where employers do this the health benefits largely disappear. Small firms with no slack are also poorly placed to absorb any of it.

On balance I still support the change, because the sectors where it works are large and the sectors where it does not can be treated differently. A blanket four-day week would be unwise. A four-day week as the default, with exceptions where the arithmetic genuinely does not work, would capture most of the benefit.
title: A four-day standard working week
